name: Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease, REN-related

clinicalPearls: A subtype of autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease caused by variants in REN (encoding preprorenin/renin), part of the ADTKD family alongside UMOD, MUC1, HNF1B and SEC61A1.
A distinctive early clue is childhood anaemia, often mild and disproportionate to renal function, reflecting reduced renin-driven erythropoietin and angiotensin signalling.
Hyperuricaemia and early-onset gout are characteristic and frequently predate significant renal impairment.
There is a tendency to hyperkalaemia and mildly low blood pressure, with susceptibility to acute kidney injury during volume depletion, reflecting an underactive renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis.
Urinalysis is typically bland with little or no proteinuria or haematuria, and kidneys are normal-sized or small and non-cystic on imaging.
Chronic kidney disease is slowly progressive, generally reaching kidney failure in adulthood and often later than in some other ADTKD subtypes.
Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone-blocking drugs are frequently poorly tolerated, worsening hyperkalaemia, hypotension and acute kidney injury, and must be used with caution.
Signal-peptide variants and variants in the prosegment or mature renin domain may differ subtly in age of onset and severity.
reference.pathophysiology: REN encodes preprorenin, which is processed to prorenin and then to renin, the rate-limiting enzyme of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system produced by juxtaglomerular cells. Disease-causing variants, classically affecting the signal peptide but also the prosegment and mature domains, cause misfolding and retention of mutant preprorenin within the endoplasmic reticulum, provoking juxtaglomerular endoplasmic-reticulum stress and cell injury with reduced renin production. The resulting hyporeninaemia lowers angiotensin II and aldosterone, explaining the tendency to hypotension, hyperkalaemia and salt wasting, and reduces erythropoietin, producing the characteristic anaemia; impaired urate excretion drives hyperuricaemia and gout. Chronic juxtaglomerular and tubulointerstitial injury leads to slowly progressive interstitial fibrosis and chronic kidney disease.
additionalDifferentials: ADTKD-UMOD (uromodulin) — also causes hyperuricaemia and gout but lacks the childhood anaemia and hypotension
ADTKD-MUC1 (mucin-1) — bland presentation caused by a characteristic frameshift, without the same gout bias
ADTKD-HNF1B — with renal cysts, hypomagnesaemia, diabetes and genital or pancreatic anomalies
Familial juvenile hyperuricaemic nephropathy of other genetic cause
Alport syndrome and thin basement membrane disease (usually with haematuria, aiding exclusion)
additionalInvestigations: Detailed family history and pedigree consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance
REN sequencing within an ADTKD gene panel (UMOD, MUC1, HNF1B, SEC61A1)
Serum urate and potassium with assessment of plasma renin and aldosterone activity, which are typically low
Full blood count to identify anaemia disproportionate to renal function
Renal ultrasound showing normal or small kidneys without numerous cysts
Bland urinalysis with quantification of any proteinuria
Kidney biopsy only if the diagnosis remains unclear, showing non-specific tubulointerstitial fibrosis
redFlags: Acute kidney injury precipitated by volume depletion, gastroenteritis or renin-angiotensin blockade
Dangerous hyperkalaemia, particularly with potassium-retaining drugs
Progressive decline in kidney function toward kidney failure
Symptomatic anaemia in a child with a suggestive family history
reference.prognosis: Chronic kidney disease progresses slowly, with kidney failure typically in mid-to-late adulthood, generally later than in ADTKD-UMOD or MUC1. Anaemia and gout are manageable, and because the defect is intrinsic to the native kidney, outcomes after transplantation are good.
pitfalls: Attributing the childhood anaemia to iron deficiency and missing the renal diagnosis
Prescribing renin-angiotensin inhibitors that precipitate hyperkalaemia, hypotension and acute kidney injury
Provoking reversible acute kidney injury through aggressive diuresis or dehydration
Expecting cysts or proteinuria and dismissing the diagnosis when they are absent
Overlooking the dominant family history of gout and chronic kidney disease
